options.text: I strongly believe that adults should have the complete personal freedom to buy dangerous items or enjoy risky hobbies if they want to. An adult should be trusted to make their own choices in life, and the government should not act like a strict parent. If a person wants to ride a fast motorcycle and fully understands the danger, they should be allowed to do so as long as they wear a helmet. True freedom means being allowed to choose your own lifestyle and accepting the results.

options.label: A3
options.text: I think the smartest approach is not a total ban, but rather a system of strict regulations and special licenses. For example, the government should not ban fireworks completely, but they should restrict their use to trained professionals during official holiday events. Similarly, people should be allowed to drive fast motorcycles, but only after passing a very difficult safety test and paying for expensive insurance. This allows personal choice while still keeping the public safe.

options.label: A1
options.text: Last autumn, my family and I went to a famous mountain near my hometown to see the colorful changing leaves. We woke up very early and spent about three hours hiking up a quiet trail surrounded by tall trees and fresh air. When we finally reached the top, the view of the valley below was absolutely beautiful and peaceful. We sat on a large rock, ate the delicious sandwiches my mom made, and took a lot of great photos together before walking down. It was a wonderful day.

options.label: A2
options.text: A few months ago, during my summer break, I went camping with my university friends near a large forest and a clean river. We set up two tents together, collected small pieces of wood from the ground, and built a warm campfire in the evening. We roasted marshmallows, looked at the bright stars in the night sky, and talked about our future goals until very late. It felt amazing to escape the noisy city streets and just enjoy the simple sounds of the trees and water.

options.label: A3
options.text: Last summer, I took a train to a quiet beach with my best friend because we were both completely exhausted from our final exams. We spent the whole afternoon walking along the soft sand, dipping our feet into the cool ocean water, and looking at the waves. We also found a small spot under some tall palm trees to sit down, listen to music, and watch a beautiful orange sunset. That simple trip to nature completely washed away all my school stress and gave me new energy.

options.label: A1
options.text: I definitely prefer to spend my vacation time deep in nature doing outdoor activities like hiking and camping. I spend most of my daily life sitting inside a crowded university classroom or staring at a computer screen, which makes me feel very tired and stressed. Going to a forest or a mountain allows me to breathe fresh air, move my body, and enjoy absolute quiet. Nature helps my mind and body relax completely in a way that a noisy, busy city never can.

options.label: A2
options.text: I strongly prefer to visit a large city to see modern museums, eat at nice restaurants, and go shopping during my free time. I think camping in nature can be very uncomfortable because of annoying bugs, unpredictable weather, and sleeping on the hard ground. Ina big city, everything is highly convenient; you can easily take the subway, visit amazing art galleries, and buy unique gifts for your family. For me, a great vacation is all about comfort, entertainment, and good food.

options.label: A3
options.text: I prefer a mix of both choices depending on how much time I have for my vacation. If I only have a short weekend break, I like to go to a nearby mountain or park to hike and clear my head quickly. However, if I have a long two-week winter break, I prefer to travel to a major global city to explore historical buildings and enjoy the fast nightlife. Doing both types of trips keeps my life exciting and helps me stay balanced as a student.

options.label: A1
options.text: I absolutely believe it is vital for crowded modern cities to spend money on planting trees and building large parks. Living in a city with only tall concrete buildings and grey roads can make people feel very depressed, lonely, and anxious. Green parks provide a safe, free space where families can walk their dogs, children can play sports, and students can read books in the fresh air. Trees also clean the dirty city air and make the neighborhood look much more beautiful and welcoming.

options.label: A2
options.text: In my opinion, cities should prioritize using land to build affordable houses and modern offices instead of large parks. Today, many young people and students cannot find a cheap apartment to live in because there is a severe shortage of buildings, which makes rent prices way too high. Using limited city land for offices also creates thousands of good jobs for young graduates. People can easily visit nature outside the city on weekends, but they need a place to live and work every single day.

options.label: A3
options.text: I think that city planners should find a smart way to combine both ideas instead of choosing just one. For example, when companies build a new apartment complex or a tall office building, the government should force them to plant trees on the roof or build a small green garden on the first floor. This way, the city can grow economically and provide enough homes for its citizens while still keeping the air clean and giving people a nice touch of nature right outside their windows.

options.label: A1
options.text: I believe that protecting nature is the direct responsibility of every individual person in society. Big changes always start with small daily actions, and if everyone stops throwing plastic trash on the ground, the earth will instantly become much cleaner. We cannot just sit around and wait for the government to fix everything for us. Taking care of your own trash, recycling plastic bottles, and respecting trees when you go hiking are simple manners that show you are a mature and responsible citizen.

options.label: A2
options.text: I strongly believe that big companies and governments should handle environmental protection because they have the real power and money to make a difference. Individual actions like recycling a paper cup are nice, but they are too small to stop global pollution. Large factories dump toxic waste into rivers and cut down entire forests every single day for profit. The government needs to create strict laws and give huge fines to these companies to force them to protect the environment and use clean energy.

options.label: A3
options.text: I think that environmental protection requires a joint effort from both individual citizens and the government. Normal people must do their part by keeping their local parks clean, picking up trash, and avoiding plastic bags when they go shopping. At the same time, the government must support these citizens by building good recycling centers and passing strict laws against industrial pollution. If individuals and leaders work together as a team, we can easily protect our beautiful nature for the future.

options.label: A1
options.text: Last semester, I had a very important group presentation in my morning English class. I had worked hard on my slides, but on the morning of the presentation, I woke up late and ran out of the house in a huge hurry. When I arrived at the classroom, I realized with absolute shock that I had completely forgotten my laptop at home on my desk. I felt terrible because my teammates were waiting for me. Luckily, a kind classmate let me borrow his computer, but it was a scary moment that taught me to pack my bag the night before.

options.label: A2
options.text: A few months ago, I mixed up the dates for my university history midterm exam. I thought the test was on a Thursday, but it was actually on Tuesday morning. I was sitting casually in the campus cafe when a friend texted me asking where I was. I had to run to the classroom as fast as I could, and I only had fifteen minutes left to finish the entire test. I got a very low grade on that exam, and it was a painful lesson that forced me to start checking my school calendar every single day.

options.label: A3
options.text: Last year, during a very busy final exam week, I completely forgot my best friend's birthday. She had invited me to a small dinner party, but my brain was so overwhelmed with studying that I totally missed it and stayed in the library all night. When she called me the next morning, I felt incredibly guilty and sad. I apologized immediately and bought her a nice gift, and we resolved the issue. It made me realize that even when life gets super busy, you must remember the people who matter most.

options.label: A1
options.text: I definitely prefer to write down quick memos on my smartphone calendar app whenever I have a busy schedule. My brain is often very tired from long lectures and studying, so it is incredibly easy for me to forget small details like meeting times or grocery lists. Writing everything down in a safe digital place clears my mind and takes away a lot of daily stress. I can just look at my phone screen and know exactly what task I need to do next without worrying about making mistakes.

options.label: A2
options.text: I strongly prefer to just trust my own brain and memory instead of constantly relying on notes or smartphone apps. I believe that your memory is like a muscle, and if you never use it, it will naturally become weak and lazy over time. By forcing myself to remember my homework deadlines, friends' phone numbers, and daily appointments in my head, I am keeping my mind sharp, active, and focused. It feels much more independent and natural to live your life without checking a screen every five minutes.

options.label: A3
options.text: I prefer to use a mix of both methods depending on how important the information is. If it is just a routine daily task, like going to the gym or meeting a classmate for lunch, I easily trust my own brain to remember it. However, if it is a major life event, like a university registration deadline or a doctor's appointment, I will immediately write a memo on my phone and set aloud alarm. This double system ensures that I never miss the big things while keeping my mind active.

options.label: A1
options.text: I absolutely think that spacing out is a very bad habit that severely hurts a student's learning and grades. Whena professor is explaining a difficult topic, missing just a few minutes of information because your mind is wandering can make you completely lost for the rest of the lecture. You will end up wasting hours of your free time later trying to relearn everything alone in the library. Staying strictly focused during class is the smartest way to study efficiently and get good grades.

options.label: A2
options.text: In my opinion, letting your mind wander occasionally can actually be very healthy for your brain and your creativity. High school and university students face an incredible amount of stress every day from constant testing and assignments. Spacing out for a few minutes gives your brain a much-needed break to relax and recharge its energy. Many great ideas and creative solutions to problems come to us naturally when we are not forcing our minds to think about a strict textbook.

options.label: A3
options.text: I think that spacing out is just a natural way the human brain protects itself when it is completely exhausted. If you try to pay absolute attention to a long, boring lecture for three hours without a single break, your brain will naturally shut down because it cannot hold that much data. Instead of fighting it, schools should provide short five-minute breaks during long classes. This would let students rest their minds naturally so they can focus perfectly when the actual teaching starts again.

options.label: A1
options.text: I completely agree that smartphones and short videos are destroying the attention span of young people today. Apps like TikTok and Instagram are designed to give your brain quick rewards in just ten or fifteen seconds, which makes traditional books feel incredibly boring by comparison. Many students can no longer sit quietly and read a single page of a textbook without feeling a strong urge to check their phone notifications. It is creating a major problem for long-term learning and deep focus.

options.label: A2
options.text: I strongly disagree with the idea that technology is destroying our minds. Young people today do not have a worse attention span; rather, they have learned how to process information much faster than previous generations. We can quickly filter through vast amounts of data online, multitask between different apps, and find the exact answers we need in seconds. Technology has just changed how our brains operate, making us more adaptable and efficient in a fast-moving modern world.

options.label: A3
options.text: I think that smartphones are just an inanimate tool, so they are not inherently good or bad for our attention span. It all depends entirely on the self-discipline of the individual student using the device. If a student uses their phone purely to watch endless funny videos all night, then yes, their focus will suffer. But if they use specialized apps to track their study time, block distractions, and listen to educational podcasts, the phone becomes an amazing tool that actually improves their mental discipline.

options.label: A1
options.text: When I started my first semester at university, I moved into my own small apartment near the campus. Suddenly, I had the ultimate freedom to stay up as late as I wanted and eat whatever I liked without my mom checking on me. However, I quickly realized that this freedom came with a lot of heavy responsibility. In the first week, I forgot to buy groceries, ran out of clean clothes, and missed an early morning lecture. It was a big wake-up call that forced me to create a strict weekly schedule for cleaning and studying.

options.label: A2
options.text: When I turned fifteen, my parents finally bought me my very first smartphone and allowed me to manage my own screen time. At first, I handled this new freedom very badly; I stayed up until 3:00 AM playing games and scrolling through social media apps every night. My school grades started to drop, and I felt tired all the time. Realizing my mistake, I decided to use an app that locks my phone automatically at 10:00 PM. Taking that responsibility helped me fix my sleep and my grades.

options.label: A3
options.text: Last year, my older brother gave me a large amount of cash as a birthday gift and told me I could spend it on absolutely anything I wanted. I felt a great sense of freedom and immediately wanted to buy expensive clothes and video games. However, I stopped myself and decided to open a separate savings account instead. I used that money to pay for a specialized computer coding course that helped me with my university studies. I felt really proud of myself for making a mature and responsible choice.

options.label: A1
options.text: I definitely prefer a society with strict government limits that prioritize public safety over total freedom. Human beings can often be careless, selfish, or short-sighted, especially when it comes to dangerous things like speeding, drinking alcohol, or using harmful chemicals. Without strict laws and clear age limits, innocent people would get hurt on the streets every single day. Having strong rules might feel a little bit annoying sometimes, but it creates a peaceful, safe, and stable neighborhood where everyone can live without fear.

options.label: A2
options.text: I strongly prefer a society that allows maximum personal freedom where individuals can make their own choices. I believe that every grown person owns their own body and life, so the government should not act like a parent by telling us what we can drink, eat, or buy. When you give the government too much control, they just create endless restrictions that ruin personal happiness and block business growth. People need the freedom to make their own mistakes so they can learn how to become truly responsible adults.

options.label: A3
options.text: I prefer a balanced approach where the government only steps in when a person’s choices directly harm other people. For example, I fully support strict laws against drinking and driving because that behavior puts innocent drivers and walkers in terrible danger. However, when it comes to personal choices that only affect the individual, like smoking or eating unhealthy food, people should have the total freedom to choose for themselves. Protecting others is necessary, but total control goes too far.

options.label: A1
options.text: I think that eighteen is the perfect age limit for all of these adult choices. In most parts of the world, eighteen is legally the age when a person finishes high school, can vote in elections, and can join the army to defend their country. If a young person is mature enough to choose the president of their nation or hold a full-time job, they are certainly old enough to decide if they want to drive a car, smoke a cigarette, or have a drink with their friends. We should treat them like real adults.

options.label: A2
options.text: In my opinion, eighteen is much too young for dangerous habits like drinking alcohol and smoking. Scientific research shows that the human brain keeps growing and developing until a person is twenty-five years old, especially the part of the brain that controls logic and danger. Teenagers who are only eighteen often make silly, impulsive choices just to show off to their classmates. Raising the legal drinking and smoking age to twenty-one would save thousands of young lives from bad car accidents and health problems.

options.label: A3
options.text: I think it is much smarter to separate these privileges into different age categories based on the actual danger involved. For example, driving a car should stay at eighteen because young people need to commute to their universities or entry-level jobs independently. However, smoking and drinking are highly addictive habits that can easily ruin a student's health and studies before their life even starts. Therefore, I believe the age limit for driving should be eighteen, but alcohol and cigarettes should be restricted until twenty-one.

options.label: A1
options.text: I believe that a person is truly free only when they have zero responsibilities and can do exactly what they want each day. When you have a full-time job, a family to take care of, or strict school rules to follow, your time does not belong to you anymore. You have to wake up at a certain hour, wear specific clothes, and follow someone else's orders. True freedom means having a completely blank schedule where you can travel, sleep, or play games whenever you feel like it, without anyone telling you no.

options.label: A2
options.text: I strongly believe that real freedom comes from actively choosing your own responsibilities in life. Having zero responsibilities sounds nice for a few days, but it quickly becomes incredibly boring, lonely, and completely meaningless. When you choose to study hard for a specific career, take care of a pet, or support your mother, you are using your freedom to build a meaningful life. Real freedom is not about acting like a lazy child; it is about having the power to decide what matters to you.

options.label: A3
options.text: I think our definition of freedom changes naturally as we grow older and move through different stages of life. When we are young high school students, freedom feels like having a long summer vacation with no homework and zero chores to worry about. But as we mature into university students and adults, we realize that a life with no goals feels completely empty. Eventually, we learn that the highest form of freedom is the ability to choose our own job, our own relationships, and our own duties.

options.label: A1
options.text: Last semester, my classmate and I had a big argument during a group project. He wanted to finish the whole assignment on the very last day, but I wanted to work on it a little bit every day because I hate rushing. We were both getting quite angry and stopped talking for a whole afternoon. That evening, I decided to text him and suggested we meet up for lunch to talk quietly. We agreed to divide the project into two parts so we could both work at our own speed. In the end, we got a great grade and stayed good friends.

options.label: A2
options.text: A few weeks ago, I had a huge argument with my older brother because he borrowed my favorite laptop without asking me first, and he accidentally spilled some water near it. I was so upset that I started yelling at him right away in the living room. He got defensive, and we didn't speak to each other for two days. Finally, my mom told us to sit down together and cook dinner. My brother apologized for being careless, and I apologized for losing my temper so quickly. We resolved it by promising to respect each other's things more.

options.label: A3
options.text: Last summer, my best friend and I were planning a weekend trip together, but we had a big disagreement about our budget. She wanted to stay in a very nice, expensive hotel, but I really needed to save my money for school books. We both felt frustrated and almost canceled the trip completely. To fix the problem, I found a clean and cozy guesthouse that was much cheaper but still located in a great area. She looked at the photos, liked the place, and we happily agreed to go there. It was a good lesson in compromising.

options.label: A1
options.text: I definitely prefer to confront the person immediately whenever an argument happens. I think it is much better to say what is on your mind right away because keeping your angry feelings inside just makes the situation feel worse over time. If you walk away, the other person might think you are ignoring them or that you do not care about the problem. Even if the conversation is a little bit emotional or difficult, speaking immediately helps clear the air so everyone can understand the truth and fix the issue before the day ends.

options.label: A2
options.text: I strongly prefer to walk away and calm down for a while before I try to talk about a conflict. When people are angry, they usually say very mean things that they do not actually mean, which can easily ruin a good relationship forever. Stepping outside or taking a few deep breaths gives my brain time to think clearly and logically about the situation. Once my angry feelings are gone, I can return to the person and have a peaceful, polite conversation to solve the issue without any shouting.

options.label: A3
options.text: I usually choose my approach depending on who I am having the argument with. If it is a small disagreement with a very close family member like my mom, I prefer to talk about it immediately because we know each other so well and can easily move past it. However, if the conflict is with a classmate or a boss at work, I always prefer to walk away and think quietly first. This helps me choose my words carefully so I do not say anything unprofessional that could cause major problems for my future.

options.label: A1
options.text: I absolutely think that arguing with strangers online is a complete waste of your time and energy. People on apps like Instagram or TikTok almost never change their minds because they are just hiding behind a screen and want to win the argument. Most online comments are very rude, and reading them just makes you feel stressed, sad, or angry for the rest of the day. It is much smarter to close the app, go outside, and spend your valuable time talking to real-world friends who actually respect your opinions.

options.label: A2
options.text: In my opinion, reading and participating in online debates can actually be a very useful way to learn about the world. In daily life, we usually only talk to people who share our exact same background and ideas. But on the internet, you can interact with people from completely different countries, ages, and cultures. Even if the argument gets a little bit intense, seeing why someone disagrees with you helps open your mind and teaches you to look at a single topic from many different sides.

options.label: A3
options.text: I think that arguing online is just a natural phase that many young people go through when they first start using social media. When you are a student, it feels exciting to share your thoughts and defend your favorite things online against critics. However, as you grow a bit older and get busier with university or work, you naturally realize that these digital fights do not matter at all in real life. You slowly stop typing long comments and start focusing your energy on your own real goals instead.

options.label: A1
options.text: I believe that conflicts are absolutely necessary for any healthy relationship to grow stronger over time. Human beings are all completely different, so it is impossible to agree on every single thing forever. If two friends never argue, it usually means someone is hiding their true feelings and pretending to be happy just to avoid trouble. Having a small, honest argument allows both people to share their real thoughts, fix hidden problems, and learn how to respect each other's differences more deeply.

options.label: A2
options.text: I strongly believe that a relationship can be perfectly healthy and happy without ever having loud arguments or fights. You do not need to get angry or yell at someone just to solve a problem in life. Two mature people can easily handle a disagreement by sitting down, listening to each other quietly, and making a calm decision together before any conflict even starts. Relationships that are based on deep peace, kindness, and gentle communication are much more stable and comfortable in the long run.

options.label: A3
options.text: I think the role of conflict changes naturally as a relationship moves through different stages over time. When two people first become close friends or start dating, they often have small arguments because they are still learning about each other's habits and boundaries. These early conflicts are useful because they help set clear rules for the friendship. But after many years pass and you know the person perfectly, the need for arguments naturally disappears because you already know how to keep each other happy.

options.label: A1
options.text: Last semester, I had to give a big presentation in front of my entire English class. I was so nervous that my hands were shaking, and I made a few silly mistakes while speaking. I felt terrible afterward and sat at my desk feeling like a total failure. During the break, a classmate came over, smiled, and told me that my pronunciation was excellent and that my presentation slides looked beautiful. That simple compliment instantly made my anxiety disappear and gave me the confidence to keep trying.

options.label: A2
options.text: A few months ago, I studied incredibly hard for a math exam but still got a very low grade. I was sitting on a bench on campus looking really sad, and my older brother noticed me. He came over, sat down, and told me that he knew how hard I worked and that one bad grade does not mean I am stupid. His kind words of encouragement reminded me that mistakes are just part of learning. It made me feel so much better, and I started studying again the next day.

options.label: A3
options.text: Recently, I spent three whole days editing a short video project for a school club, and I was exhausted and worried that it wasn't good enough. When I finally showed it to the club leader, she clapped her hands and told me I did a fantastic job and that I havea real talent for making creative things. Hearing those sweet words made all my tiredness wash away instantly. It felt amazing to know that my hard work was noticed and appreciated by someone else.

options.label: A1
options.text: I definitely prefer people to give me direct and honest criticism whenever I make a mistake. Soft words might make me feel comfortable for a minute, but they do not help me improve my skills or fix the actual problem. If my school work is bad, I want to know exactly what is wrong right away so I can correct it and get a better grade next time. Honest feedback saves a lot of time, and I believe it is the fastest way to learn and grow as a student.

options.label: A2
options.text: I strongly prefer to receive soft, gentle encouragement when I make a mistake. When I fail a task, I usually already know that I did badly, and I feel very stressed and upset with myself. If someone criticizes me directly right away, it just ruins my confidence and makes me want to give up completely. Kind and gentle words help calm my mind first, which makes it much easier for me to listen to advice later and try again with a positive attitude.

options.label: A3
options.text: I prefer a mix of both methods, which many people call a feedback sandwich. First, I like it when people give me alittle bit of gentle encouragement so I know they still support me and respect my effort. After that, they can give me the direct, honest criticism about what parts of my project need to be fixed immediately. Ending with a kind word keeps my motivation high while still giving me the practical information I need to succeed.

options.label: A1
options.text: I believe that giving children too many compliments can actually make them weak and lazy. If a child hears that everything they do is perfect, they will never learn how to handle failure or work hard to overcome difficulties in real life. When they grow up and enter the real world, they will feel shocked and deeply hurt the first time a teacher or a boss criticizes them. Praise should be given only when a child truly does something special, not for every little thing.

options.label: A2
options.text: In my opinion, saying kind words and praising children constantly is the absolute best way to build their self-esteem. The world can be a very scary and harsh place for a young child who is still learning how to do basic things. Constant encouragement makes them feel safe, loved, and brave enough to try new hobbies, like drawing or playing sports, without being afraid of making mistakes. A confident child who feels supported by their family will always try harder in school.

options.label: A3
options.text: I think the answer depends entirely on what you are praising. If you constantly tell a child they are naturally smart or talented, it can make them weak because they will stop trying hard. However, if you praise their actual effort and hard work—like saying “I am proud of how long you practiced today”—it is very healthy. This kind of specific compliment teaches children that success comes from dedication, which helps them stay strong when facing tough challenges later.

options.label: A1
options.text: I find it much easier to accept critical advice from a teacher or a classmate. School relationships are more professional, so when a teacher tells me to fix a mistake, I know it is strictly about my work and not a personal attack on who I am. Family members, like parents, often bring too many emotions into the conversation, which can make their criticism feel like lecturing or nagging. It is much easier to stay calm and listen logically when the feedback comes from school.

options.label: A2
options.text: I definitely think it is easier to take negative feedback from a close family member like my mom or brother. Even if their words are a little bit sharp or painful to hear, I know deep down in my heart that they love me completely and only want what is best for my future. Classmates or teachers might not truly care about me personally, so their criticism can sometimes feel cold or mean. I can trust my family's honesty 100% because their advice always comes from a place of love.

options.label: A3
options.text: I think both types of criticism are difficult to hear at first, but we naturally learn to need both as we grow up. When we are young children at home, our parents' corrections teach us basic manners and how to be a good person. But as we grow into university students, we need the objective, professional feedback of our professors to fix our academic mistakes. Accepting criticism from different people is just a normal part of becoming a mature and successful adult.

options.label: A1
options.text: My grandfather has had a massive influence on my life and daily habits. Even though he is in his late seventies, he still wakes up at 5:00 AM every single morning to go for a long walk and read the daily newspaper. Watching him maintain this absolute discipline taught me that true success in life isn't about sudden bursts of luck, but rather the small, consistent actions you take every day. His amazing work ethic motivates me to stay highly organized and focused on my university studies even when I feel incredibly lazy.

options.label: A2
options.text: An older woman who lives next door to my family has been a wonderful mentor to me since I was a child. She lost her husband a few years ago, but she still manages to tend her garden every afternoon with a huge smile on her face and always stops to greet me warmly. She taught me the valuable life lesson that we cannot always control the difficult events that happen to us, but we can always choose our attitude toward them. Her resilient, positive mindset completely changed how I handle school stress.

options.label: A3
options.text: When I was struggling with immense anxiety about choosing my university major, a retired high school teacher took the time to sit down with me. He told me about all the completely different career paths he had traveled throughout his long life before finally finding his true passion in education. His story taught me that it is perfectly okay to not have your entire life figured out at the age of twenty. He helped me realize that growing older is a slow process of discovery, which instantly took a giant weight off my shoulders.

options.label: A1
options.text: I definitely prefer to enjoy my lifestyle to the fullest right now without constantly stressing over strict rules. Iama firm believer in the YOLO mindset—you only live once—so wasting my youth counting calories or refusing to eat delicious fast food with my friends sounds incredibly boring. Of course, I try to stay somewhat active, but I refuse to let the fear of getting old ruin my current happiness. Life is far too short and unpredictable to spend your best years eating plain salads and denying yourself simple daily pleasures.

options.label: A2
options.text: I strongly prefer to strictly manage my diet and exercise routine right now so I can guarantee a long, vibrant, and healthy future. The choices we make during our youth directly build the foundation for our old age, and I don't want to suffer from chronic illnesses later just because of temporary cravings today. Eating nutritious meals and working out daily gives me incredible brainpower and energy for my current studies anyway. For me, true freedom isn't about eating junk food; it’s about ensuring my body stays strong and independent for decades to come.

options.label: A3
options.text: I prefer to take a balanced middle-ground approach that combines both philosophies. During the busy school week, I am highly disciplined; I pack healthy meals, avoid sugar, and make sure to hit the campus gym regularly to keep my energy up. However, when the weekend finally arrives, I completely relax my rules, hang out with my classmates, and eat whatever I want without feeling a single bit of guilt. This strategy protects my long-term health while still letting me enjoy the fun, carefree side of being young.

options.label: A1
options.text: I absolutely think that being young today is far more stressful due to the brutal academic competition and the constant pressure of social media. In my parents' generation, you could easily secure a stable, high-paying job with a basic university degree, but today, students need perfect grades, multiple internships, and fluent foreign languages just to get an entry-level interview. options.label: A2

Nowadays, people just stare at a blue dot on their screens instead of looking at the actual streets and landmarks around them. If their phone battery dies, they become completely helpless and have no idea where north or south is. We don't practice memorizing routes anymore because technology does all the heavy lifting for us. It has made our brains a bit lazy when it comes to understanding geography. We are losing a basic human skill because we rely too much on satellites.

options.label: A2
options.text: I don’t think technology has made us worse; it has actually made us much more confident explorers. In the past, people were afraid to visit new neighborhoods because they were worried about getting hopelessly lost. Now, because of GPS, people are willing to travel to unfamiliar places and try new things without fear. It gives us the safety net we need to step out of our comfort zones. Even if we don't memorize the streets, we are still successfully navigating the world every day. It's just a modern tool that makes life much more efficient.

options.label: A3
options.text: I think technology has changed how we navigate, but it isn't necessarily a bad thing. On one hand, it’s true that we don't memorize street names or look at physical maps like our parents did. On the other hand, we can travel through foreign countries effortlessly without getting stressed or losing time. It saves us from a lot of unnecessary arguments and confusion during family trips. Our brains might be adapting to a digital world rather than losing a skill. It’s a fair trade-off because the convenience is worth it.

options.label: A1
options.text: It is definitely much better to stop and ask a local person for assistance right away. Local people know the area perfectly and can give you the fastest, safest shortcuts that aren't on a map. Trying to figure it out on your own usually just wastes time and can sometimes lead you into dangerous neighborhoods. Asking for help is also a great way to interact with the community and experience local kindness. It takes away the panic immediately because you are no longer facing the problem alone. It’s the most logical and efficient choice.

options.label: A2
options.text: I believe it is better to try and figure it out on your own first. When you solve a navigation problem by yourself, you learn the layout of the city much better. Looking at your surroundings and finding landmarks forces you to pay attention and grow more independent. If you always run to someone else for help, you will never develop a strong sense of direction. Plus, language barriers can sometimes make asking locals very confusing and stressful. It is much more rewarding to find your own way out of a situation.

options.label: A3
options.text: I don't think there is a single right answer because getting lost is just part of life and how we grow. Everyone has a different comfort level, and we learn by making mistakes and finding our own solutions in the moment. If you are in a hurry, asking someone is a quick fix, but if you have time, wandering around can be a great lesson. You can't learn to handle stressful situations if you are always following a perfect set of instructions from a teacher or a stranger. Managing the situation on your own terms is how you truly become an experienced traveler.

options.label: A1
options.text: I definitely put money into savings right away. As soon as I get paid, I move a small amount to a separate account so I can't see it. It makes me feel secure knowing that my future is taken care of. Then, I can spend whatever is left without feeling guilty about it.

This method works for me because I never have to worry about being late on my bills. It is a very practical way to handle a tight budget.

options.label: A1
options.text: I think technology makes it much harder to save money nowadays. Apps like Amazon and food delivery services make spending way too fast and convenient. options.label: A3
options.text: I think technology is a tool that can be used for both good and bad spending. If you use shopping apps and save your credit card info, you will probably spend too much. options.label: A1
options.text: I strongly believe that schools should be required to teach financial management. Most students graduate with no idea how to pay taxes or how interest rates work. options.label: A1

options.label: A1
options.text: I think flexible hours are much better for students today. Everyone learns at different times; some people are night owls and others work best very early in the morning. options.text: I definitely think it’s beneficial. It’s not just about the music; it’s about discipline. You can’t get good at an instrument overnight, so it teaches kids that they have to work for their success. Plus, playing in a school band or orchestra is a great way to make friends and learn how to work as a team.

options.label: A3
options.text: I believe music education is a vital part of a well-rounded curriculum. Beyond the artistic value, studies show that learning an instrument can improve a child's cognitive development and mathematical skills. It provides a creative outlet that is often missing from more academic subjects like science or history.

options.label: A1
options.text: Yes, I think it is still very important. Even though a computer can make music easily, it is not the same as a human playing a real instrument. When a person plays, they put their feelings into the music. It is a special skill that takes many years to learn, and I think we should still value that hard work.

options.label: A2
options.text: That’s an interesting point. It’s true that anyone can make a beat on a laptop now, but I don't think that replaces the soul of a real instrument. Playing a guitar or a piano is a physical experience—you can feel the vibration and the emotion. I think people will always appreciate real musicians because there is a level of talent there that a computer just can't copy.

options.label: A3
options.text: I believe there is room for both. While digital music production has made creating music more accessible to everyone, the discipline of learning a physical instrument offers unique benefits. It develops fine motor skills and a deep patience that you don't necessarily get from using software. In my view, technology is a great tool, but the human element of playing an instrument remains irreplaceable.

options.label: A1
options.text: Yes, I like children very much. I think they are very funny and they have a lot of energy. I come into contact with them quite often because my older sister has two young kids. I usually visit them on the weekends to play games or watch movies together. It is always a very happy time for me.

options.label: A2
options.text: To be honest, I like kids, but only in small doses. I find them really creative and fun to talk to, but they can be quite exhausting if you spend too much time with them. I don't see them very often in my daily life, so I mainly just see them when I'm out at the park or the mall.

options.label: A3
options.text: I would say I have a neutral but positive view of children. I appreciate their curiosity and the way they see the world. As for how often I see them, it’s quite rare. My social circles are mostly adults, so I only really come into contact with children during family gatherings or holiday events. I enjoy those moments, but I’m also happy to return to my quiet routine afterward.

options.label: A1
options.text: My favorite memory is playing in the park with my grandfather every Sunday. He used to buy me an ice cream after we played on the swings. It is a very happy memory for me because the weather was always sunny and I felt very safe and loved. I still remember the taste of the vanilla ice cream.

options.label: A2
options.text: I'd have to say my favorite memory is our family camping trips during the summer. We would go toa lake far away from the city, and I loved sitting by the campfire at night. Looking back, it was a really special time because there were no phones or distractions—just us hanging out and enjoying nature together.

options.label: A3
options.text: A particularly fond memory I have is learning how to ride a bicycle for the first time. I remember feeling quite nervous, but my father was very patient and encouraged me until I could balance on my own. It sticks in my mind because it was my first real sense of independence and achievement as a young child.

options.label: A1
options.text: Yes, I think it is very difficult. In the past, life was simpler. Now, parents have to worry about the internet and social media. Also, everything is more expensive today, like food and education, so parents have to work very hard. It takes a lot of energy to be a good parent.

options.label: A2
options.text: I think it’s much more challenging than it used to be. Even though we have better technology and medicine, the mental pressure on parents is huge. You have to monitor what your kids see online and protect them from things like cyberbullying. options.label: A3
options.text: Raising children has always been a demanding task, but the challenges have shifted. While we no longer face many of the physical hardships of the past, we now deal with complex issues like digital safety and intense academic competition. It requires a lot of patience and adaptability to guide a child through such a fast-paced environment.

options.label: A1
options.text: Legally, most people become adults at eighteen, but I think it is different for everyone. Some people are very mature at sixteen because they have a job. Other people are still like children at twenty-five. I think you become an adult when you start taking care of yourself and paying your own bills.

options.label: A2
options.text: I don't think there’s a specific magic number. Even though the law says eighteen, I feel like you only truly become an adult when you take full responsibility for your actions. For some, that happens early because of their life circumstances. For others, it takes a bit longer to lose that childish mindset and start thinking about the future.

options.label: A3
options.text: In my view, the transition from childhood to adulthood is a gradual process rather than a sudden change. While eighteen is the age of legal responsibility, emotional maturity often develops much later. I believe a person becomes an adult when they can make independent decisions and understand how those decisions affect others around them.

options.label: A1
options.text: Actually, I don't enjoy housework at all. It feels like a waste of time because the house just gets dirty again the next day. The chore I dislike the most is washing the dishes. I hate the feeling of wet food on my hands, and it takes a long time to dry everything and put it away.

options.label: A2
options.text: To be honest, I’m not a fan of cleaning, but I do it because I can't stand living in a mess. I find vacuuming okay because you can see the results immediately, but I absolutely hate doing the laundry. The whole process of washing, drying, and then folding clothes feels like it takes an entire day. I wish I could just hire someone to do it for me!

options.label: A3
options.text: I have a bit of a love-hate relationship with housework. While I find the actual labor quite tedious, I really appreciate the sense of calm I feel when the house is tidy. However, the chore I find most difficult is cleaning the bathroom. It’s a very physically demanding task, and I usually try to put it off as long as possible.

options.label: A1
options.text: Yes, I think children should help. It teaches them how to be responsible and how to take care of themselves. If they help with small things like setting the table or cleaning their room, they will be more independent when they grow up and live in their own apartment.

options.label: A2
options.text: Definitely. I think it’s a mistake for parents to do everything for their kids. Doing chores teaches children that they are part of a team and that everyone has to contribute. It’s not about making them work hard; it’s about giving them life skills so they aren't shocked by how much work it takes to runa home when they become adults.

options.label: A3
options.text: I believe it’s beneficial for children to have some domestic responsibilities. It instills a sense of discipline and respect for the environment they live in. However, I don't think they should be overwhelmed with chores. It should be a balance where they help out enough to learn the value of hard work, but still have plenty of time for their studies and play.

options.label: A1
options.text: Yes, I think it is fair for everyone to help. If everyone lives in the house and makes a mess, everyone should help clean it. When people share the work, the cleaning is finished much faster, and then everyone has more time to relax together. It is about being a good team.

options.label: A2
options.text: I think it really comes down to who has the most free time. In many homes today, both people are working full-time, so it’s only practical to split the chores. options.label: A3
options.text: I believe the distribution of housework should be based on a fair agreement between those living together. Rather than following traditional roles, it’s more effective to look at each person's schedule and strengths. If one person is busier with work, the other might take on more at home, and vice versa. The most important thing is that the arrangement feels balanced and that everyone contributes in some way to the home.

options.label: A1
options.text: I hope so! I already have a robot vacuum and it helps a lot. It is great because it works while everyone is out. I think in the future, we will have robots to cook our food and fold our laundry too. It will give us much more free time to enjoy our lives.

options.label: A2
options.text: I think we’re heading in that direction, but we aren't there yet. Robot vacuums are great for floors, but they can't clean windows or scrub a kitchen counter. I’m waiting for the day when a robot can actually organize my closet! Technology makes things easier, but I think humans will always have to do at least a little bit of the tidying up.

options.label: A3
options.text: While technology has certainly made domestic life more convenient, I doubt it will ever completely replace human effort. Robots are excellent for repetitive, simple tasks, but they lack the judgment needed for deep cleaning or organizing personal items. I see technology as a helpful assistant rather than a total replacement for the care we put into our own homes.

options.label: A1
options.text: My favorite way to relax is just staying in bed and watching movies on my laptop. I like to order some food so I don't have to cook, and I just stay in my pajamas all day. It is the best way for me to forget about my school stress and recharge my energy for the next week.

options.label: A2
options.text: I’m a big fan of “unplugging” on my days off. I usually head to a local park with a book, find a nice spot under a tree, and just read or people-watch for a few hours. I try to leave my phone in my bag so I’m not constantly checking messages. For me, doing nothing means getting away from screens and just enjoying the fresh air.

options.label: A3
options.text: I actually find that “doing nothing” is an art. I prefer to spend my free time without any specific goals. I might listen to some music or spend a long time making a cup of coffee. It’s not about being lazy; it’s about giving my brain a break from the constant need to achieve something. It helps me feel much more refreshed than if I were out running errands.

options.label: A1
options.text: I prefer a completely free day. During the week, my life is very busy with classes and homework, so I havea strict schedule. On the weekend, I don't want to look at a clock. I like to wake up whenever I want and decide what to do in the moment. It makes me feel more free.

options.label: A2
options.text: I actually prefer having at least a bit of a plan. If I have a completely free day, I usually end up wasting it scrolling on my phone, and then I feel guilty at the end of the night. Even if it’s just one or two small goals, like going to the gym or meeting a friend, having a schedule makes me feel like I’ve actually used my time well.

options.label: A3
options.text: I think a balance is best, but I lean toward having a free day. While a planned schedule is great for productivity, it can feel like work. A free day allows for “spontaneity,” which means I can do things based on how I feel in the moment. I believe having that flexibility is essential for preventing burnout and keeping life interesting.

options.label: A1
options.text: Yes, I agree. Everywhere we look, people are talking about working hard and making more money. Even on social media, everyone shows their “perfect” busy lives. I think this makes people feel bad if they are just resting. We need to remember that humans are not machines; we need time to just be quiet.

options.label: A2
options.text: Absolutely. There’s this idea now called “hustle culture” where if you aren't starting a business or learning a new skill in your free time, you're failing. It’s pretty exhausting. I think it leads to a lot of unnecessary stress and anxiety because we feel like we always have to be “on.”We've forgotten that resting is actually a productive thing to do for our health.

options.label: A3
options.text: I believe there is a significant amount of pressure to be constantly productive, largely due to how connected we are through technology. Since we can work from anywhere, the line between office time and home time has disappeared. While being productive is important for progress, I think society often ignores the fact that rest is actually what allows us to perform well in the long run.

options.label: A1
options.text: Yes, I think it is a great idea. If people work four days and have three days off, they will be much happier. They will have more time for their family and their hobbies. When they go back to work on Monday, they will have more energy and probably do a better job than people who are tired all the time.

options.label: A2
options.text: I’m all for it. Most of the studies I’ve read show that people are actually just as productive in four days as they are in five because they focus better. Plus, it would reduce commuting costs and help the environment. I think it would solve a lot of the 'burnout' issues we see in big companies today.

options.label: A3
options.text: It’s a complicated issue, but I support the idea in theory. A 4-day work week could significantly improve mental health and work-life balance. However, it might be difficult to implement in certain industries, like healthcare or emergency services. Perhaps instead of a strict rule, companies should offer more flexible options so employees can choose a schedule that fits their needs.

options.label: A1
options.text: I prefer to save money for the future. I think it is important to have a “safety net” in case of an emergency. If I spend all my money on trips or expensive food now, I might have problems later when I want to buy a house or a car. Saving money makes me feel calm and secure.

options.label: A2
options.text: I’m definitely more of an “experience” person. I believe that memories from traveling or going to concerts stay with you forever, while money just sits in a bank. Of course, I try to save a little bit, but I’d rather use my youth to see the world and learn new things instead of waiting until I'm too old to enjoy them.

options.label: A3
options.text: I try to find a balance between the two. While I agree that saving for future goals like retirement or a home is essential, I also think that life shouldn't be only about work and saving. I usually set aside a specific portion of my income for savings, and whatever is left, l use to enjoy life today. That way, I'm prepared for the future without missing out on the present.

options.label: A1
options.text: I think the most important factor is hard work. You can be very smart, but if you are lazy, you will not succeed. A person who shows up on time and finishes their tasks will always be respected by their boss. Consistency is the key to getting a promotion.

options.label: A2
options.text: To me, it’s all about networking and communication. You can be the most talented person in the room, but if you don't know how to talk to people or build relationships, it’s hard to get ahead. Most opportunities come from the people you know, so being a ‘people person' is a huge advantage in any career.

options.label: A3
options.text: I believe adaptability is the most critical factor today. The world is changing so fast because of technology, so you have to be willing to learn new skills constantly. If you stay stuck in your old ways, you'll be left behind. Success comes to those who can pivot and stay curious throughout their professional life.

options.label: A1
options.text: I prefer to buy high-quality items, even if they are expensive. For example, if I buy a cheap pair of shoes, they might break in two months. But if I buy expensive ones, they can last for years. In the long run, I actually save money because I don't have to keep buying new things.

options.label: A2
options.text: It depends on what I’m buying. For things I use every day, like a phone or a winter coat, I’ll invest in quality. But for things that go out of style quickly or that I only need for a short time, I’ll go with the cheaper option. I don't see the point in spending a fortune on something I’m only going to use a few times.

options.label: A3
options.text: I generally support the idea of “buying less, but buying better.” I think it’s better for the environment and for my own finances to own a few well-made items rather than a lot of cheap, disposable ones. High-quality products usually function better and feel more special, which makes me appreciate them more.

options.label: A1
options.text: I agree that success is having a job you love. We spend most of our lives at work, so if we are unhappy, even a lot of money cannot make us feel better. If you enjoy what you do, you will wake up happy every morning. To me, that is the real meaning of a successful life.

options.label: A2
options.text: I'll be honest—I think you need a bit of both. You can love your job, but if you can't pay your rent, you're going to be incredibly stressed. However, I’ve seen people with huge salaries who are totally miserable. I think success is reaching a point where you have enough money to be comfortable, but you also don't hate what you do every day.

options.label: A3
options.text: I believe success is subjective, but I lean toward the idea of personal fulfillment. A high salary is great, but it often comes with extreme stress and very little free time. To me, being successful means having a balance—having a career that challenges and interests you, while also having enough time and resources to enjoy your life outside of work.

options.label: A1
options.text: My favorite sport to watch is basketball. I like it because it is very fast and exciting. Every minute, someone is scoring a point, so I never get bored. I also like to play it with my friends at the park on weekends because it helps us stay active and have fun together.

options.label: A2
options.text: I’ve always been a huge fan of tennis. I find it fascinating to watch the strategy and the mental strength of the players. It’s not just about hitting the ball; it’s like a game of chess on a court. I don't play it very well myself, but I never miss the big tournaments on TV.

options.label: A3
options.text: Honestly, I’m not really interested in watching any sports, and I don't follow any professional teams. However, I do enjoy swimming quite a lot. Even though I'm not a “sports fan,” I value the way swimming keeps me healthy.

options.label: A1
options.text: I prefer team sports like soccer. I like being part of a group and working together to win a game. If Iam tired, my teammates can encourage me to keep going. It is also a great way to make new friends and learn how to communicate with other people.

options.label: A2
options.text: I’m definitely more into individual sports. I like the feeling that my success depends entirely on my own effort. When I go for a run, I don't have to wait for anyone else or follow a team schedule. I can just put on my headphones and focus on beating my own personal records.

options.label: A3
options.text: I think both have their advantages, but I usually lean toward individual sports for my daily routine. options.label: A1
options.text: I think they are very good for children. Competitive sports teach kids that you have to work hard to get a result. They also learn how to follow rules and respect their coach. Even if they lose, it is a good lesson because they learn how to try again and not give up.

options.label: A2
options.text: I’m a bit worried about the pressure. It’s great for kids to stay active, but sometimes parents and coaches take it too seriously. options.label: A3
options.text: It really depends on the environment. Competition can be a healthy motivator that teaches children resilience and discipline. However, if the focus is entirely on winning, it can lead to burnout or a loss of self-esteem. As long as the adults involved keep the atmosphere positive and supportive, I think the benefits outweigh the risks.

options.label: A1
options.text: Yes, I think they deserve it. Their careers are very short, usually only ten or fifteen years. They also have to train every day and they risk getting hurt. Since millions of people pay to watch them, it makes sense that they get a share of that money.

options.label: A2
options.text: To be honest, I think the salaries are getting a bit out of control. It seems crazy that an athlete earns more in a week than a doctor or a teacher earns in a year. While I know they are talented, I think that money could be used better to support local community centers or school sports programs.

options.label: A3
options.text: I have mixed feelings. On one hand, professional sports is a massive industry that generates billions of dollars, and the athletes are the stars of the show. On the other hand, the gap between their pay and ‘normal jobs is quite shocking. I think it’s fair that they are paid well, but perhaps the extreme, multi- million dollar contracts are a bit excessive.

options.label: A1
options.text: I enjoy visiting museums because they are very quiet and peaceful. It is a great way to learn about history and see beautiful things from the past. I especially like history museums because they help me understand how people lived a long time ago. It feels like traveling back in time.

options.label: A2
options.text: To be honest, I find museums very boring. The last time I actually visited one was on a school field trip back in middle school, and I remember it being quite dull. Maybe now that I'm older, I would appreciate the art and history a bit more.

options.label: A3
options.text: I have mixed feelings about museums. While I appreciate that they preserve our culture and heritage, I often find the traditional galleries a bit exhausting. I don't visit them often because I prefer more active hobbies. That being said, if I were traveling to a new city, I would probably stop by a major museum just to see the most famous pieces and learn a little bit about the local history.

options.label: A1
options.text: I prefer going with friends. It is more fun to look at the exhibits and talk about them together. If I see something interesting, I can share it with my friends immediately. After the museum, we can go to a cafe and talk about our favorite parts of the day.

options.label: A2
options.text: I actually prefer going by myself. options.label: A3
options.text: It really depends on the type of museum. If it’s an art gallery, I prefer solitude so I can really reflect on the pieces. However, if it’s a science or history museum, it’s much more enjoyable to go with a group. Having others there to discuss the information with makes the whole experience more engaging and social.

options.label: A1
options.text: I think museums should be free for everyone. If they are free, more people will go to learn about art and history. Many families cannot afford expensive tickets, so free museums would give every child a chance to see famous paintings and learn new things.

options.label: A2
options.text: That’s a tough one. On one hand, making them free would definitely encourage more people to visit. But on the other hand, museums need money to pay for staff, security, and cleaning. Maybe a good middle ground would be to have “free days” once a month or keep them free for students and seniors.

options.label: A3
options.text: I believe the world’s most famous collections, like the Louvre, should be more accessible to everyone. Currently, these museums are incredibly expensive and often overcrowded, which makes it difficult for students to visit. Perhaps they could offer lower prices for the general public while relying on government support to cover the high costs of security and preservation.

options.label: A1
options.text: I don't agree. Even though we can see pictures of art on the internet, it is not the same as seeing it in real life. When you stand in front of a giant statue or an old painting, it feels very different. Museums are special places that a computer screen cannot replace.

options.label: A2
options.text: I can see why some people think that, but I totally disagree. The internet gives you information, but museums give you an experience. There’s a certain atmosphere in a museum that you just can't get from a website. Plus, it’s nice to get away from screens for a while and see something physical and real.

options.label: A3
options.text: To some extent, I agree. For someone like me, I can't easily travel to Europe or other distant places to visit those famous museums in person. The reality is that travel is expensive and takes a lot of time, so! usually just browse the collections on my phone instead. I wish I could be there to see the art for myself, but since that isn't possible right now, having everything online is a great alternative. For me, the internet is enough.

options.label: A1
options.text: I prefer cooking for myself because it is much cheaper than eating at a restaurant, and I can choose exactly what I want to eat. The reality is that I am usually too busy with work, so I cannot cook as often as I want.

options.label: A2
options.text: To be honest, I really don't enjoy cooking at all. I definitely enjoy eating, but the actual process of preparing food is just not for me. options.label: A3
options.text: I actually enjoy a mix of both. I find cooking to be a very creative hobby, so I try to prepare my own meals during the week to stay healthy even though it’s just a simple meal. options.label: A1
options.text: Yes, I think it is very important. If you can cook, you can take care of your health and save a lot of money. You don't have to rely on other people for food. It is a basic skill that every adult should have.

options.label: A2
options.text: I definitely think it's a vital life skill. You don't need to be a professional, but knowing the basics helps you understand what is actually going into your body. Plus, it’s a great way to save money. Being able to whip up a quick meal is much better than eating frozen food every night.

options.label: A3
options.text: I believe it’s an essential skill for independence. When you know how to cook, you have more control over your nutrition and your expenses. It also allows you to share your culture with others through food. Even if someone doesn't enjoy it, knowing the fundamentals is important for staying healthy.

options.label: A1
options.text: Yes, I think it is changing. Many people are very busy now, so they prefer to buy fast food or microwave meals. It is much faster than traditional cooking, which can take many hours. I worry that children will not learn their family recipes.

options.label: A2
options.text: I think it’s a bit of a double-edged sword. On one hand, people definitely rely more on delivery apps because life is so fast-paced. options.label: A3
options.text: I believe traditional cooking is evolving rather than disappearing. While convenience food is more common now, many people are also becoming more interested in home-cooked meals for health reasons. Technology, like air fryers, actually makes it easier for busy people to cook at home, so I don't think we will lose the habit completely.

options.label: A1
options.text: Yes, I think food is the best way to learn about a new country. When you try a traditional dish, you can understand the history and the ingredients of that place. It is a fun way to experience a different culture without even traveling there.

options.label: A2
options.text: Absolutely. I think food is a universal language. Even if you don't speak the language of a country, sharing a meal helps you connect with the people there. Every dish tells a story about the climate and the traditions of a culture. For me, trying local street food is always the highlight of any trip abroad.

options.label: A3
options.text: I agree that food is a powerful tool for cultural exchange. It provides a unique insight into how people live and what they value. When we explore international cuisines, we become more open- minded and appreciative of global diversity. It’s a sensory experience that teaches us more thana history book ever could.

options.label: A1
options.text: I see advertisements every day on my phone, especially on YouTube and Instagram. Usually, I do not pay nfjch attention to them because I want to watch my video. I often click the 'skip' button as fast as I can because I find them a bit annoying.

options.label: A2
options.text: They are everywhere, but I notice them most on social media. The technology is so good now that the ads usually show me things I actually like. I wouldn't say I love them, but occasionally I’ll stop and look if the product looks interesting or if the video is well-made.

options.label: A3
options.text: To be honest, I try to ignore most advertising, but it's becoming harder because they are part of almost every app. I see them on websites, public transport, and social media. I rarely pay close attention to them unless the advertisement is very creative or shows something I really need.

options.label: A1
options.text: Yes, I recently bought a new pair of running shoes because I saw an ad on Facebook. The shoes looked very cool and they were on sale. I am happy with my purchase because they are very comfortable, so the advertisement was actually helpful for me.

options.label: A2
options.text: Actually, no. I never buy things directly from ads because I find them quite annoying. I’m a very careful shopper, so instead of clicking the ad, I go to my favorite shopping app, read all the customer reviews, and then decide for myself if it's worth it.

options.label: A3
options.text: I try to be a careful shopper, but I have been influenced by ads before. For example, I once signed up for a language learning app after seeing a very persuasive ad online.
